page: Hubble examines Cloud-9, first of new type of object
text:
Radio observations first picked out a compact cloud of neutral hydrogen near the spiral galaxy Messier 94. Its round form sets it apart from many of the larger, irregular hydrogen clouds studied near the Milky Way.

Astronomers used Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys to look for a faint population of stars. They found none, supporting the interpretation of a gas cloud dominated by dark matter. It could reveal what conditions were like before a galaxy begins forming stars.

> Nicknamed “Cloud-9,” this is the first confirmed detection

> Reionization-Limited H I Cloud, or "RELHIC.”

page: New Discovery Challenges Evolution of Galaxy Clusters
text:
ALMA found unexpectedly hot gas between galaxies in a cluster that was still taking shape early in cosmic history. The team detected this atmosphere by measuring how electrons in the hot gas distort the cosmic microwave background.

The atmosphere contained more thermal energy than models predicted for a cluster at that stage. Outbursts from accreting black holes in the forming cluster are one possible source of the additional heat.

> hot gas in a forming galaxy cluster, SPT2349-56.

> the universe was just 1.4 billion years old

page: Webb pushes boundaries of observable Universe closer to Big Bang
text:
The team used Webb's near-infrared spectrograph to check the distance previously estimated from images. The spectrum showed how far cosmic expansion had stretched the galaxy's light, letting researchers place the observation in cosmic history.

The researchers found unusually abundant nitrogen and noted a similar signature in some of the Milky Way's oldest stars. The galaxy also appears to have begun ionizing nearby hydrogen, a clue to when starlight could travel more freely in the early Universe.

> the newly confirmed galaxy, MoM-z14,

> a bright galaxy that existed 280 million years after the Big Bang.

page: NASA Telescopes Spot Surprisingly Mature Cluster in Early Universe
text:
Webb found candidate member galaxies in a region where Chandra independently detected hot gas. The infrared and X-ray observations together support the interpretation that the galaxies belong to a cluster in the process of forming.

The system is visible roughly a billion years after the Big Bang. An extended hot atmosphere at such an early stage gives astronomers a test of how quickly large cosmic structures can grow.

> The object, known as JADES-ID1

> Webb sees at least 66 potential members

page: A Solar System in the making? Two planets spotted forming in disc around young star
text:
WISPIT 2 is a young star surrounded by an extended disc of dust and gas. After the earlier discovery of the giant planet WISPIT 2b, observers identified a second object much nearer the star. The team combined images from SPHERE with interferometric measurements to test its planetary nature.

Both planets sit in gaps between dusty rings. A narrower gap farther from the star could point to an additional forming planet, but the observations did not establish that it exists.

> The new planet — WISPIT 2c — is four times closer

> The team then used the GRAVITY+ instrument on the VLTI

page: Milky Way's fastest star orbits our supermassive black hole so closely it feels its spin
text:
The Very Large Telescope Interferometer found a star on a tight orbit around Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's central black hole. Its closest pass is about twelve astronomical units from the black hole. The star then travels faster than eight percent of the speed of light.

Relativity predicts that a rotating black hole alters the motion of nearby objects. Following the star across its approximately 8.7-year orbit could eventually let astronomers measure the black hole's spin.

> The star, named S301,

> reaches speeds of 25 000 km/s

page: New ‘exomoon’ detection challenges cosmic labels
text:
Researchers found evidence of a candidate satellite with an estimated mass no lower than Jupiter's in a young system. A substellar companion more than thirty times as massive as Jupiter sits between the star and the candidate in the orbital hierarchy. The team studied the system using the CRIRES+ spectrograph on the VLT.

The proposed orbit motivates the satellite label despite its giant-planet mass. The finding is evidence for a candidate and awaits confirmation.

> a moon-like object in the CD-35 2722 system.

> Instead, it circles a brown dwarf

page: Faintest planet ever imaged from Earth found after more than 10 years of hide-and-seek
text:
A VLT team studying the giant Beta Pictoris b noticed another faint source in its images. ESO archive exposures going back as much as eleven years helped confirm that the separate source was a third planet in the system.

The third planet orbits farther from the star than its two known siblings and has a mass of about 2.4 Jupiters. It is relatively cold, which contributes to the difficulty of identifying it in images against the light of its host star.

> The new planet, Beta Pictoris d,

> is 100 times fainter than Beta Pictoris b

page: Researchers discover hundreds of cosmic anomalies with help from AI
text:
ESA researchers applied a neural network to roughly one hundred million image cutouts from the Hubble Legacy Archive. The model ranked the cutouts by how unusual they appeared, and astronomers inspected promising candidates by eye.

Interacting galaxies accounted for much of the resulting collection, which also included gravitational lenses and galaxies trailing gas. Some objects remained hard to classify. The work illustrates how automated screening can help specialists find rare targets in large image archives.

> Their neural network, which they named AnomalyMatch,

> In just two and a half days, AnomalyMatch completed its search

page: Largest image of its kind shows hidden chemistry at the heart of the Milky Way
text:
Radio measurements from ALMA were assembled into a mosaic of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone. The images show cold gas and dust near the central black hole, from long filaments down to small clouds near individual stars.

The survey distinguishes dozens of molecules, including organic compounds. Researchers can use these observations to investigate how stars form in an environment affected by massive stars and their explosions.

> ACES — the ALMA CMZ Exploration Survey

> The region featured in the new image spans more than 650 light-years.

page: Astronomers surprised by mysterious shock wave around dead star
text:
RXJ0528+2838 is an accreting white dwarf in a binary with a Sun-like star. After an image from the Isaac Newton Telescope showed a nebula, researchers used MUSE on the VLT to study the gas. The follow-up linked the bow shock to the binary.

The observations suggest a sustained outflow even though no accretion disc is evident. A strong magnetic field may contribute to the outflow, but the measured field alone does not explain how the shock persisted for the inferred duration.

> The star RXJ0528+2838 is located 730 light-years away

page: Webb locates former star that exploded as supernova
text:
After the supernova was detected in 2025, researchers compared earlier Webb and Hubble images of NGC 1637 to locate the progenitor. Webb's infrared cameras revealed a red supergiant where the explosion was seen. Obscuring dust had kept the star out of the Hubble images.

That finding offers a reason why the progenitors of some supernovas are difficult to identify in archived observations and motivates searches for other red supergiants concealed by dust.

> Applying computer models to the Webb observations indicated that the dust is likely carbon-rich

page: ALMA and VLA Reveal a Vast Reservoir of Star-Forming Fuel in a Galaxy Near Cosmic Dawn
text:
The VLA observed faint carbon monoxide emission from REBELS-25, a galaxy seen roughly 700 million years after the Big Bang. That emission traces cold molecular gas, which supplies the material for new stars.

ALMA measurements of emissions from gas and dust helped characterize the environment and cross-check the gas estimate. The observations show that some galaxies had gathered a large fuel supply for star formation at this early epoch.

> the team derived a molecular gas mass of roughly 100 billion solar masses

page: Hubble Details Early Galaxy Transforming Neighborhood
text:
Hubble identified a distant galaxy that was releasing ionizing ultraviolet light when the universe was young. Compact groups of young stars might have cleared a path through surrounding neutral gas, which would ordinarily absorb those photons.

The observation puts this kind of light escape earlier than previously identified examples. It helps explain how young galaxies could have changed the gas between galaxies from opaque to transparent.

> The galaxy, cataloged MXDFz4.4, existed at the end of the Era of Reionization

page: Webb studies how a planet survived death of its star
text:
Webb observed WD 1856 b as it passed in front of its white dwarf. Comparing the transit at different wavelengths allowed researchers to estimate how much infrared radiation the exoplanet contributes.

The planet was warmer than expected from the white dwarf's illumination alone. Cooling models favor a history in which the planet stayed outside the star's red giant envelope and migrated inward later. The observations also suggest clouds and possible methane.

> a Jupiter-sized exoplanet orbiting the white dwarf every 34 hours

page: NASA’s TESS Mission Finds Planetary System in New Way
text:
TESS usually searches for periodic dimming when a planet passes in front of a star. In this case it found a giant planet by microlensing, in which a foreground system briefly magnifies a more distant star.

Gaia also observed the event, but its measurements were too widely spaced to reveal the planet. The more frequent TESS observations captured additional structure in the brightness curve.

> it recently detected a planet about 40,000 light-years away

page: NASA's Chandra Unveils Mysterious X-ray Objects
text:
A search of Chandra's public archive identified objects in six galaxies that appear in low-energy X-ray images and disappear at higher energies. The researchers inferred that these objects also emit intense ultraviolet radiation. They found examples both near sites of star formation and among older stars.

Their nature remains uncertain. One possibility is a compact object accreting matter from a companion. The sources could help explain how gas between stars becomes ionized in some galaxies.

> The researchers found a total of 84 of these “hypersoft X-ray sources”

page: Euclid discovers new comet
text:
Software designed to detect moving objects flagged a streak in Euclid's September images. Its changing position helped the team recover the object in other exposures. Diffuse material around it indicated a comet rather than an inactive body.

Ground observers followed up after the team checked existing catalogues and reported the discovery. The result shows how a survey aimed at distant galaxies can also identify nearby moving Solar System objects in its images.

> C/2026 S1 (Euclid) is the first new comet that Euclid has discovered.

page: Dead star and planetary bodies: astronomers spot unique disc of debris that foretells Solar System’s future
text:
Using the VLT's X-Shooter instrument, astronomers found two concentric gaseous debris rings separated by a gap around the white dwarf J1328−1450. The inner ring is richer in magnesium than the outer one, suggesting that material in the rings may come from objects with different compositions.

The study proposes two surviving rocky bodies on separate orbits. The announcement's opening compares the possible size of one object to Pluto. The detailed discussion places the inner body at roughly asteroid size and mentions Earth's Moon as another possibility for the outer body.

> shaped by two planetary bodies, one possibly as big as Pluto

page: NASA's Chandra Finds Source of Star's Mysterious Outbursts
text:
Chandra observed an unstable massive star in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559 that has repeatedly brightened over several years. The X-ray observations support the idea of a compact companion that draws in some gas when the stars pass close together.

That companion could be a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole. Gas heating up as it approaches the compact object offers an explanation for how the recurring optical outbursts and X-rays could be related.

> is pulling material from AT 2016blu every 113 days as they orbit one another.
